name: High-risk pregnancy and screening results
one_line: A high-risk label or screening result means extra care, not that something is wrong. Here is what it means and what comes next.
who_this_is_for: For anyone told their pregnancy is high risk, or whose double marker, NT scan or quadruple marker result came back as high risk.
red_flags: Severe headache, blurred vision or sudden swelling of face or hands

faq.q: What does a high-risk screening result mean?
faq.a: Screening tests like the double marker with NT scan (the combined test) or the quadruple marker estimate likelihood. They do not diagnose anything. A high-risk result means your doctor will offer more tests to get a clearer answer.

faq.q: What is the difference between screening and diagnostic tests?
faq.a: Screening tests, like the combined test or NIPT, sort pregnancies into lower and higher likelihood. Diagnostic tests, like CVS or amniocentesis, look at the baby's chromosomes directly and give a clear answer. Diagnostic tests carry a small risk of miscarriage, so your doctor talks it through with you first.

faq.q: What makes a pregnancy high risk?
faq.a: Common reasons include high BP, diabetes, thyroid problems, being over 35, twins, a previous caesarean or early birth, or a screening result that needs follow-up. Each reason calls for different care. The label simply means your team will watch more closely.

faq.q: Why have I been sent to a fetal medicine specialist?
faq.a: Your gynaecologist may refer you for detailed scans or tests. This is routine after a high-risk screening result. It is a step towards answers, not a sign that something is wrong.

faq.q: Can I still have a normal delivery?
faq.a: Often, yes. A high-risk label does not by itself mean a caesarean. Your doctor decides the safest way to deliver closer to the time.
